source.locator: lines 38-45, examples of primitive recursive relations

findings.finding: The source calls x <= y the less-than relation, although both the displayed symbol and the IsZero(x truncated-subtraction y) definition express less-than-or-equal.
findings.controlling_evidence: For natural numbers, truncated subtraction x truncated-subtraction y is zero exactly when x <= y; it is not zero exactly when x > y.
findings.required_translation_handling: Name the displayed relation less-than-or-equal and add an adjacent OLTECRREM-001 disclosure.

findings.finding: The third case changes the parameter vector of m_R from vec x to vec z, even though z is the bound search variable and every other defining clause uses vec x.
findings.controlling_evidence: The proposition and the recursive definition immediately below both define m_R(vec x,y); the third case must preserve those parameters.
findings.required_translation_handling: Use m_R(vec x,y+1)=y+1 in the third case and add an adjacent OLTECRREM-002 disclosure.

findings.finding: The parenthetical explanation of x not-divides y reverses dividend and divisor by referring to the remainder when dividing x by y.
findings.controlling_evidence: The surrounding definition says x divides y exactly when y is an integer multiple of x, equivalently when y divided by x has remainder zero.
findings.required_translation_handling: Refer to the remainder when y is divided by x and add an adjacent OLTECRREM-003 disclosure.

findings.finding: Two occurrences put the argument x inside the function-name macro as fn{nextPrime(x)}, unlike the actual application fn{nextPrime}(x) used in the recurrence.
findings.controlling_evidence: The recurrence p(x+1)=nextPrime(p(x)) and the chapter-wide convention separate a function name from its parenthesized arguments.
findings.required_translation_handling: Use fn{nextPrime}(x) consistently and add an adjacent OLTECRREM-004 disclosure.

findings.finding: The proof chooses the largest prime p_n <= x without treating x=0 or x=1, for which no such p_n exists.
findings.controlling_evidence: The claimed bound still holds in both omitted cases because 2 <= x!+1; the product-of-primes argument is valid after restricting it to x>=2.
findings.required_translation_handling: Dispatch x=0 and x=1 directly, apply the product argument for x>=2, and add an adjacent OLTECRREM-005 disclosure.

findings.finding: The asserted injective map is printed as an empty tuple applied to (a_0,...,a_k), equated to the tuple code, rather than as a map from the input sequence to its code.
findings.controlling_evidence: The preceding product defines the numeric code, and the following prose explicitly says different sequences are mapped to different numbers.
findings.required_translation_handling: Write (a_0,...,a_k) maps-to tuple{a_0,...,a_k} and add an adjacent OLTECRREM-006 disclosure.

source.locator: lines 144-168, sequence bound and bounded-search concatenation

findings.finding: The bound p_{k-1}^{k(x+1)} is undefined for the empty sequence k=0, and the subsequent minimization searches strictly below a quantity proved only to be an inclusive upper bound.
findings.controlling_evidence: The chapter fixes 0 as the empty-sequence code, so 1 is a valid bound at k=0. For k=1 with sole element x, the code 2^{x+1} equals the stated bound, showing that strict search can omit the required code.
findings.required_translation_handling: Define the bound as 1 at k=0 and the displayed prime-power expression at k>0; search through values less than or equal to the bound; add an adjacent OLTECRREM-007 disclosure.

findings.finding: The prose describes hSubtreeSeq(t,n) as containing subtrees exactly n levels from the root, but its recurrence retains the previous sequence and adds the next level, so it is cumulative.
findings.controlling_evidence: The base contains t, each successor value concatenates the preceding value with immediate subtrees, and the final claim uses hSubtreeSeq(t,t) as the sequence of all subtrees.
findings.required_translation_handling: Describe hSubtreeSeq(t,n) as containing subtrees at distance at most n and add an adjacent OLTECRREM-008 disclosure.

source.locator: lines 48-57, g_f recursion and h application

findings.finding: The source defines g_f(s,k) using entries 0 through k inclusive and then calls it with k=len(s), which reads the out-of-range entry (s)_{len(s)} and can append a spurious value.
findings.controlling_evidence: Earlier the chapter states that a sequence of length k has entries 0 through k-1. A fold over its first k entries therefore needs an empty base and must add entry k at the k-to-k+1 step.
findings.required_translation_handling: Use g_f(s,0)=emptyseq and g_f(s,k+1)=g_f(s,k) concat f((s)_k), retain the call g_f(s,len(s)), and add an adjacent OLTECRREM-009 disclosure.

source.locator: lines 27-48 and 55-89, universal cfind family and diagonal proof

findings.finding: After defining cfind_e by a partial-recursive expression for every natural e, the source introduces an extra case in which e is not an index at all and lets that inconsistent case drive the final paragraph of the diagonal proof.
findings.controlling_evidence: For every e, U(mu s T(e,x,s)) is a partial recursive function (possibly nowhere defined), so e indexes that member of the universal family. With h(e,x)=1 exactly when cfind_e(x) is defined, both h(e_d,e_d)=1 and h(e_d,e_d)=0 directly contradict cfind_{e_d} approximately-equals d.
findings.required_translation_handling: Remove the impossible non-index disjunct, state the two direct diagonal contradictions, and add an adjacent OLTECRREM-010 disclosure.
